procedural_history.originating_court: Different Benches of the High Court
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the High Court (presumably adverse to the appellant-Complainant)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Different Benches of the High Court issued orders.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant-Complainant approached the Supreme Court, aggrieved by the High Court's orders, through Special Leave Petitions (SLPs). The Supreme Court granted leave and heard the matters as Criminal Appeals. The appeals arising out of the petitions for special leave to appeal are disposed of on the terms mentioned in the judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising jurisdiction under Section 439(1) of the Cr.P.C for granting regular bail in favour of the respondents in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

facts: The case involved allegations that the accused, due to previous enmity, indiscriminately fired at the complainant and his two sons, resulting in the death of both sons and serious injuries to his nephew.
The complainant and three eyewitnesses testified, specifying the roles of the accused in the incident.
The accused had a previous criminal history.
One of the accused, while on bail for a prior offense, allegedly committed the double murder of the complainant's sons.
There were allegations that three of the accused threatened a key eyewitness in open court, which led to the registration of a new FIR.
The police filed a closure report in a cross-FIR that had been filed by the accused persons.
law: Under Section 439(1) of the Cr.P.C., the High Court has wide discretionary power to grant bail.
However, this discretion must be exercised by considering the relevant facts and principles that conventionally govern bail applications.
Courts are duty-bound to consider factors such as the gravity of the offense, the accused's criminal history, the evidence against them, and the potential for witness tampering.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had "completely lost sight of the principles that conventionally govern a Court’s discretion" when granting bail.
The Supreme Court determined that the High Court had failed to consider several crucial factors:
1. It ignored the consistent testimony of the complainant and eyewitnesses who specified the roles of the accused.
2. It overlooked the accused persons' previous criminal history.
3. It failed to account for the grave allegation that one of the accused committed the double murder while already on bail for another offense.
4. It did not consider the allegations of witness intimidation by the accused in open court.
5. It overlooked the period of custody in relation to the gravity of the alleged offense.
The Supreme Court concluded that when all these factors were examined collectively, the accused did not deserve the concession of bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting regular bail to the respondents. The Court held that the High Court's orders suffered from grave infirmity, as they failed to consider multiple critical factors. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed and set aside the impugned bail orders and directed the respondents to surrender.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising jurisdiction under Section 439(1) of the Cr.P.C for granting regular bail in favour of the respondents in the facts and circumstances of the present case.
appellant_arguments: The State of Uttar Pradesh, supporting the appellant-complainant, argued that the High Court failed to consider a relevant fact.
respondent_arguments: The fact that similar orders have been passed by the Single Judge has been relied upon.
The first respondent should not be penalized for the High Court’s failure to record adequate reasons.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court's duty to consider the circumstances of a case cannot be fulfilled by merely reciting legal formulations; the specific facts of the case must be considered and applied.
obiter: Not all legal circumstances will weigh in the same direction in a given case.

Merely recording that the court has had regard to the nature of the accusation, the severity of the punishment, the nature of supporting evidence, prima facie satisfaction of the court in support of the charge, reformative theory of punishment, and the mandate of Article 21 is not a satisfactory method of giving reasons.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in granting bail because its orders were unsatisfactory and completely lost sight of the principles that govern a court's discretion in such matters. The High Court failed to consider numerous critical factors, including the seriousness of the offense, consistent eyewitness accounts specifying the accused's roles, the accused's prior criminal history, grave allegations of committing a double murder and threatening witnesses while on bail, the short period of custody, and the fact that a cross-FIR filed by the accused resulted in a police closure report. When examined collectively, these factors demonstrated that the respondents did not deserve the concession of bail.
legal_tests_applied: In determining whether bail should be granted in a matter involving a serious criminal offence, the Court is duty bound to consider: (i) The seriousness and gravity of the crime.
Bail once granted, ought not to be cancelled in a mechanical manner – However, an unreasoned or perverse order of bail is always open to interference by the superior Court.

Bail can be revoked by a superior Court if it transpires that the courts below have ignored the relevant material available on record or not looked into the gravity of the offence or the impact on the society resulting in such an order.
The duty to consider the circumstances of the case cannot be obviated by setting down legal formulations.

Merely recording that the Court has had regard to the nature of the accusation, the severity of the punishment in the case of conviction, the nature of supporting evidence, prima facie satisfaction of the Court in support of the charge, reformative theory of punishment and the larger mandate of Article 21 is not a satisfactory method for the simple reason that the facts of the case have to be considered.
why_respondent_won: The High Court ignored that the complainant stuck to his version as recorded in the FIR and even after entering the witness-box, the complainant and three eyewitnesses specified the roles of the accused in the entire incident.
The High Court also overlooked the fact that the accused had previous criminal history.
The High Court overlooked that one of the accused while on bail, is alleged to have committed the double murder of the complainant’s son.
The High Court overlooked allegations that three of the accused threatened one of the key eye-witnesses in open Court, and an FIR was registered.
The High Court also overlooked the period of custody of the accused for such a grave offence alleged to have been committed by them.
The High Court overlooked that in the cross-FIR filed by accused persons, closure was filed by the police.
The manner in which the Single Judge of the High Court disposed of the application for bail is unsatisfactory.
policy_considerations: The judicial discretion of the High Court to give reasons or not to give reasons while granting bail is a systemic issue, as the present case is not the only one where reasons are not assigned, and it is likely that similar orders will be passed in the future.
